rv.q: Overall, it's an ambitious, carefully orchestrated work that raises the bar on technological innovation.

Full of moving scenery, lights, projections, film and magical illusions, but devoid of actual magic, the Broadway production of 'Ghost' is a lumbering megatuner with little to offer beyond a limitless array of dazzling effects.
The songs, the story and the acting are paint-by-numbers primers that add nothing to the movie.
The songs are forgettable, the dialogue is clunky, and the special effects, while impressive, can't make up for the show's fundamental dramatic weaknesses.
It is just as flavorless and lacking in dramatic vitality as many that have come before.

Turns out plenty in this leaden stage musicalization of the supernatural romantic thriller, a flavorless hash that is unrelentingly loud, vulgar and stunningly tone-deaf to the ways in which the world has changed since that era of sweet young yuppie innocence.
There is so much wrong with "Ghost," it's hard to know where to start.
In that case, I'll say, it's theater that really works.
Ghost succeeds best when it remembers that it's supposed to be a musical, and that the relationships between the characters should drive the action rather than the reverse.
Like Spider-Man Turn Off the Dark, the musical version of Ghost haunts the eye, not the ear.

Unsurprisingly, Rob Howell’s physical production (with video and projections by Jon Driscoll, illusions by Paul Kieve, lighting by Hugh Vanstone and sound by Bobby Aitken) vastly overwhelm the slim plot.
But the lyrics, co-written by Rubin and the composers, are more likely to make you laugh than cry.
Warchus has turned a touching silver-screen love story into an overly flashy showbiz musical that betrays the intimacy of its source.
Although the video projections are slick and impressive, they quickly become overwhelming, reducing the film's romantic intimacy into bloated and dizzying spectacle.
It’s a crying shame “Ghost” gets it so wrong.

cn.t: Critics find this film-to-stage adaptation technically dazzling but emotionally hollow, with impressive special effects that can't compensate for forgettable songs, clunky dialogue, and a fundamental lack of theatrical heart.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
